Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/AP View image in fullscreen Víctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973. Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/AP Chile Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile John Bartlett in Santiago Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.27 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara , the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice. Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man. Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment. The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news. “However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.” Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was detained in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 12 September 1973, the day after Gen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coup to depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende. View image in fullscreen Víctor Jara’s widow, Joan, who died in 2023, was a British dancer and activist who set up a foundation in her late husband’s name. Photograph: Roberto Candia/AP Jara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga. Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule. At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire. His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time. After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence. He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene. Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015. View image in fullscreen Pedro Barrientos being deported from the US to Chile in 2023. Photograph: Policia de Investigaciones de Chile/Reuters Sentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life. Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and was deported back in December 2023 , more than a decade after his extradition was first sought. One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!” Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application. Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice. Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Assim Alkhawaja outside court in San Diego in June, waiting for one of his many immigration check-ins. Photograph: Amanda Ulrich View image in fullscreen Assim Alkhawaja outside court in San Diego in June, waiting for one of his many immigration check-ins. Photograph: Amanda Ulrich After the raids US immigration He has a work permit, a coffee shop – and an ICE ankle monitor: ‘Is this America?’ Business owner Assim Alkhawaja was arrested by ICE as he dropped off Lyft passengers at a military base. Now he’s stuck in a terrifying fight to stay in the US Amanda Ulrich in San Diego Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google D eep within the bowels of San Diego’s federal courthouse, Assim Alkhawaja sat on the floor outside a nondescript office, waiting to be called for his ICE-mandated immigration appointment. He stared straight ahead, his posture tense, his face a mask. The hallway was brown, as was the carpet. Above Alkhawaja’s head hung a framed stock photo of a waterfall. A few paces away, official government signs encouraged people without legal status to self-deport. “Leave on your own terms,” they read, in several languages. “Claim a free flight and an exit bonus for each member of your family.” A woman emerged from behind the office door. “Assim?” Alkhawaja went in and the door closed behind him. The 53-year-old knew that, in the past, others in his situation had been detained and deported on the spot at these types of check-ins, without warning. Staff, who work for a program that is overseen by ICE , ask him the same questions here nearly every week: where do you live? Do you work? Occasionally: why are you applying for asylum? This time, there was a new one: how are you feeling? ICE agents descended on a cannabis farm. The lives of an army vet, a farm worker and professor changed for ever Read more But that question was more difficult to answer. For months, Alkhawaja, originally from Saudi Arabia, had felt a swirling cocktail of fear and anger, a disturbing sense that he’d been treated like an animal. In February, ICE agents arrested and detained him while he was dropping off two Lyft passengers at Camp Pendleton, the sprawling military base in San Diego county. At first, Alkhawaja, who was working as a ride-share driver to make extra money, thought it was a misunderstanding – that he might even receive an apology. He has a valid work permit, a pending asylum case, no criminal convictions, a doctorate from the University of San Francisco, and a popular local coffee business that’s growing steadily. View image in fullscreen Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton in Oceanside, California. Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty Images Those things didn’t matter. Alkhawaja spent the next eight days in an ICE detention center and was placed in removal proceedings. His left ankle was strapped with a bulky GPS tracker, the kind that is typically only given to high-risk individuals on parole, like registered sex offenders. He must report to immigration officials on an almost-weekly basis, either at the courthouse or via home visits, to prove that he hasn’t absconded. “I keep questioning myself,” Alkhawaja said, sitting in the sun outside the San Diego courthouse, sporting both the ankle monitor and a stylish quilted jacket. “Is this America?” After ICE raids swept southern California and the rest of the country last summer, and then continued over the past year, thousands like Alkhawaja face a new normal: legal battles that will span months or years, constant monitoring by immigration officials, and a reset of their daily lives. All of it could end in deportation. While more high-profile ICE raids in Los Angeles garnered national headlines last June, San Diego has also continued to see a constant, if not quieter, drumbeat of arrests – at the courthouse , Home Depots , military bases and outside schools . ICE has removed more than 16,000 people from the San Diego region alone between January 2025 and April of this year. And this summer, arrests across the nation have picked up again , with a record number of immigrants arrested since Trump took office for the second time. Chart of immigration arrests in San Diego increasing during the summer of 2025 and remaining high “It ebbs and flows, when [and where] arrests happen. Sometimes it happens outside of a courthouse, sometimes it happens in the streets,” said Sydney Johnson, an associate attorney who works at an immigration law firm in San Diego. Johnson and the firm are representing Alkhawaja and his case. “The tactics change, but the goal is the same – to make it harder for people to want to fight their case here, and to make them just give up.” ‘Like cattle’ in a detention center On the morning of his recent immigration appointment, a balmy southern California weekday in June, Alkhawaja shapeshifted between several different personas in the span of a few hours: asylum seeker fighting to stay in the country, business owner making sure his nascent coffee shop stays afloat, and brother and friend trying to “live like normal”. That day, he drove straight from the courthouse to a San Diego shipping facility, where he was picking up bags of coffee beans imported from specialty farms in Brazil and Colombia. Alkhawaja owns a nearby coffee cart called Sands Coffee Roasters, a small, family-run business that’s expanded into a neighboring brick-and-mortar shop over the past year. As Alkhawaja helped load half a dozen burlap sacks of coffee beans into the back of his pickup truck, he looked different than he had an hour before. He was animated, smiling, wearing a new outfit. Workers called him “sir” as they brought out his coffee order. “I’m more confident here,” he said. “We switch, we have to survive.” When he first applied for asylum in 2024, Alkhawaja assumed immigration officials would consider this side of his life: the plans for his new business, his background in higher education. “That’s what I thought,” he said. “That I would be considered a good immigrant.” View image in fullscreen Anti-ICE protesters outside the Edward J Schwartz federal building in San Diego in January. Photograph: Carlos A Moreno/Anadolu via Getty Images But a new reality began to unspool in February, at the entrance to the county’s largest military base, according to a sequence of events retold by Alkhawaja. That night, around 6pm, Alkhawaja first pulled up to the main gate of Camp Pendleton. He and all other drivers entering the base were asked to show their driver’s licenses. Alkhawaja had never given Lyft rides to the base before, but it also didn’t cross his mind to be worried. He handed over his valid license to a guard, who scanned it. “Wait a minute,” the man told him, and he disappeared back inside the guardhouse. Alkhawaja’s two Lyft passengers waited nervously in the back seat. When the guard returned, he asked for another form of ID. Alkhawaja handed over his active work permit, which expires in February 2030. This time, the guard left again, he said, but returned with two ICE agents, who asked Alkhawaja if he had a court date for his asylum case. He replied that he did not. “You’re coming with us,” they told him, according to his retelling. Alkhawaja was informed that, yes, he was actively being arrested, he said. Then he was handcuffed: his wrists and ankles, connected by a chain that wrapped around his waist. “It was as if I assassinated the president,” he said. ICE raided their city, taking parents, spouses and friends. That’s not where it ends Read more Camp Pendleton has worked specifically with ICE agents since at least 2025, when the base launched a “security initiative” with ICE to support “identity verification and access screening operations”. Across the county, ICE arrests at military bases have spiked . Johnson, Alkhawaja’s attorney, said his experience matched what she’s heard from others who have been arrested and detained at Camp Pendleton. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security wrote in an email that immigration officers “have the authority to question, without warrant, any alien or person believed to be an alien concerning his or her right to be, or to remain, in the United States”. During the arrest, the agents took Alkhawaja’s phone, all of his IDs (including his Costco card) and the shoelaces from his shoes, he said. He was put in a van – with the restrictive handcuffs, he had to jump to get inside – and was driven to an office in downtown San Diego. Once there, he said an agent offered him $3,000 to leave the country immediately , rather than be detained. He refused. Later that night, another van took him to the Otay Mesa detention center, one of the largest immigration detention facilities in California, where he’d spend more than a week. “We’re like cattle, animals,” Alkhawaja said of the center. “The process of transferring the detainee is really unhuman.” View image in fullscreen The Otay Mesa detention center. Photograph: Meg McLaughlin/San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images Inside the facility, Alkhawaja said, officials took the rest of his belongings: his hat, belt, jacket. He was given a uniform to wear for the duration of his stay: navy blue, with “DETAINEE” printed on the back in big block letters. He was then assigned to a room with eight other people, where the fear was palpable. Alkhawaja and the others didn’t know when they would be released, or if they would be transferred to other detention centers across the country. Alkhawaja spent the next week settling into a kind of routine. Wake up. Go to the bathroom (detainees couldn’t use the restroom during the night, he said). Stand out in the yard. Watch the Fox News that was being played on the communal TVs. Return to the rooms to be counted. The drinking water smelled and tasted bad, he said, and it felt like everything cost money: phone calls, snacks, hygiene products. CoreCivic, the company that manages Otay Mesa , maintained in an email that the “safety, health and wellbeing of the individuals entrusted to our care is our top priority,” and that their water comes from “the same municipal source used by the surrounding San Diego community”. How Alkhawaja was even able to be put in removal proceedings, while having a valid work permit and an open asylum case, comes down to a widening “grey area” between what is considered lawful and unlawful in ever-evolving immigration law, Johnson said. Asylum seekers can apply for and receive a specific type of work permit while their cases are pending, she said, but obtaining that permit doesn’t mean they technically have “legal status” in the US. “It puts people in a bad spot, where they’re like: ‘But I did the right thing, I applied for asylum within the timeframe, and it’s not my fault that it’s pending,’” she said. But that’s the unfortunate truth, Johnson added: “You can do everything right and you can still get screwed.” In response to questions about how Alkhawaja’s arrest on the military base unfolded, the DHS spokesperson, who described him as “a criminal illegal alien from Saudi Arabia”, argued that Alkhawaja had also been arrested for “disorderly conduct” more than two decades prior. “All of his claims will be heard by a judge,” the spokesperson said. “Despite his criminal history, this illegal alien was released on bond pending immigration proceedings.” The fact that DHS had seemingly dug up an old unrelated arrest, and one that did not end with any convictions, was deeply unnerving to Alkhawaja. He explained that in 2002, while on a trip to the US, he and an American friend were enjoying a night out in San Diego when they started chatting with a woman, who Alkhawaja later pieced together was an undercover police officer and was posing as a sex worker. Suddenly police cars surrounded the duo and they were arrested, but Alkhawaja said he was swiftly released once they got to the station. The whole situation was extremely confusing, he said, because he had been a bystander to the initial conversation and, to his knowledge, was never actually charged with a crime. Johnson confirmed that Alkhawaja has no criminal convictions on his record. “I believe they are bringing this up to try to justify their actions,” she said of the DHS comments. “The reality is a 2002 arrest when he was visiting his family here, without more, does not bar him from seeking asylum.” As for conditions within Otay Mesa, the DHS spokesperson said that detainees in ICE facilities are provided with “proper meals, quality water, blankets, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers”. The dream of ‘living normally’ In June, by the time Alkhawaja showed up to Sands Coffee Roasters with the fresh shipment of beans, customers were already filtering in and out, ordering Turkish coffee, flavored lattes and freshly baked cookies. Inside the store were typical coffee accoutrements: a commercial espresso machine, a big stainless steel roaster, display cases for baked goods. But there were also personal touches hanging on the wall: a photo of Alkhawaja’s family’s ancestral home in Palestine, and a traditional Palestinian embroidery, called tatreez, that his mother had made for him. The center of the embroidery read, in Arabic: “May Allah protect you.” Translating that message, the weight of his current situation pulled down on Alkhawaja again. He hasn’t seen his mother, who now lives elsewhere in the Middle East, for two years. Whenever she asks him when he’s coming to visit, Alkhawaja tells her what she wants to hear. Maybe after the summer, he says, or some other time down the road. View image in fullscreen Assim Alkhawaja works inside Sands Coffee Roasters, a small business he owns in Oceanside, California. Photograph: Amanda Ulrich Recently, Alkhawaja has often returned to another common worry: that he will now be viewed as a politicized caricature of a detained immigrant, as a “miserable, defeated person”. How, exactly, he ended up here has been mystifying to him. “I wasn’t thinking that one day in my life I will live like this,” he said. Alkhawaja is Palestinian, but he was born and raised in Saudi Arabia. He finally made the decision to apply for asylum, after years of visiting family and studying in the US, because he feared for his life back home. (Alkhawaja and Johnson requested that specific details of his asylum case be withheld due to safety concerns.) The next official hearing in his case is scheduled for October. Since launching his fight to stay in the country, one thing has surprised Alkhawaja: the fact that people care. When he emerged from Otay Mesa, he was shocked to see that a GoFundMe had been set up on his behalf, and was gaining traction. On a different day, dozens of mothers from a local activist group drove over to his coffee shop, kids in tow, to show support and hear his story. Other strangers now trickle into the store. “We heard about you,” many have told Alkhawaja, he said, “and we just want to tell you that this is not right.” If he’s granted asylum, Alkhawaja’s plan is to continue running the coffee shop, to “live normally, like others”. “I want here to be home,” he said. “I started, and it’s hard to start again somewhere else.” But in the end, it’s not up to him. Next week, and the weeks after that, as he heads to his perpetual immigration check-ins, Alkhawaja’s family members will wish him good luck before he leaves, as they always do. “It’s as if”, he said, “I’m going to a battlefield.” Explore more on these topics US immigration After the raids San Diego California US politics West Coast features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2026/9/.text: Daily Kos Community 9/11: America Can’t Let the War Lies Go Down the Memory Hole Again by Thom Hartmann Community This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication. Friday, September 11, 2026 at 8:22 AM PDT Recommend Story Share: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Save 10 Comments Add Daily Kos to Google Image by Thomas Wolter from Pixabay Today is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the event that first brought America together and then was cynically exploited by George W. Bush and Dick Cheney to steal Iraq’s oil, following their illegal invasion of Afghanistan for pure politics just a bit more than a year earlier. Yet the media today (so far, anyway) is curiously silent about Bush and Cheney’s lies. Given the costs of both these wars — and Netanyahu and Trump using October 7th in a similar fashion to justify this insane war with Iran — it’s an important moment to discuss our history of wars, both illegal and unnecessary, and those that are arguably essential to the survival of democracy in the world. To be clear, I support US involvement — and even an expanded US involvement — in the defense of the Ukrainian democracy against Putin’s Hitler-grabs-Poland-like attack and mass slaughter of Ukrainian civilians. Had the world mobilized to stop Hitler when he invaded the Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia in 1938 there almost certainly wouldn’t have been either the Holocaust or WWII, which is why Europe is so united in this effort. If Putin succeeds in taking Ukraine, his administration has already suggested that both Poland and Moldova are next, with the Baltic states (Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia) also on the menu. That would almost certainly lead to another war in Europe. And China is watching: a Putin victory in Ukraine will encourage Xi to try to take Taiwan. Between the two — war in both Europe and the Pacific — we could find ourselves in the middle of World War III if Putin isn’t stopped now. That said, essentially defensive military involvement like with Ukraine or in World War II have been the exception rather than the rule in American history. We’ve been far more likely to have presidents lie us into wars for their own personal and political gain than to defend ourselves or other democracies. For example, after 9/11 in 2001 the Taliban that then ran Afghanistan offered to arrest Bin Laden, but Bush turned them down because he wanted to be a “wartime president” to have a “successful presidency.” The Washington Post headline weeks after 9/11 put it succinctly: “ Bush Rejects Taliban Offer On Bin Laden .” With that decision not to arrest and try Bin Laden for his crime but instead to go to war, George W. Bush set the US and Afghanistan on a direct path to disaster (but simultaneously set himself up for re-election in 2004 as a “wartime president”). To further complicate things for Bush and Cheney, the 9/11 attacks were not planned, hatched, developed, practiced, expanded, worked out, or otherwise devised in Afghanistan or by even one single citizen of Afghanistan. That country and its leadership in 2001, in fact, had nothing whatsoever to do with 9/11, as I detailed in depth here on August 15th of last year. The actual planning and management of the operation was done out of Pakistan and Germany, mostly by Khalid Sheik Mohammed. The Taliban were bad guys, trashing the rights of women and running a tinpot dictatorship, but they represented no threat whatsoever to America or our allies. Almost two decades later, though, then-President Trump and Mike Pompeo gave the Taliban everything they wanted — power, legitimacy, shutting down 9 of the 10 US air bases in that country to screw incoming President Joe Biden, and allowed the release of 5000 of Afghanistan’s worst Taliban war criminals — all over the strong objections of the democratically elected Afghan government. Trump did this so could falsely claim, heading into the 2020 election, that he’d “negotiated peace” in Afghanistan, when in fact he’d set up the debacle that happened around President Biden’s withdrawal from that country. ”The relationship I have with the Mullah is very good,” Trump proclaimed — after ordering the mullah who then named himself President of Afghanistan — freed from prison over the furious objection of Afghan’s government, which Trump had cut out of the negotiations. Following that betrayal of both Afghanistan and America, Trump and the GOP scrubbed the record of their embrace of the Taliban from their websites, as noted here and here . And the conservative Boris Johnson administration in the UK then came right out and said that Trump’s “rushed” deal with the Taliban — without involvement of the Afghan government or the international community — set up the difficulties Biden faced. “The die was cast,” Defense Minister Ben Wallace told the BBC , “when the deal was done by Donald Trump, if you want my observation.” So, Republican George W. Bush lied us into both the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, and then Donald Trump tried to lie us out of at least one of them. But this was far from the first time a president has lied us into a war. — Vietnam wasn’t the first time an American president and his buddies in the media lied us into a war when Defense Secretary Robert McNamara falsely claimed that an American warship had come under attack in the Gulf of Tonkin and LBJ went along with the lie. — Neither was President William McKinley lying us into the Spanish-American war in 1898 by falsely claiming that the USS Maine had been blown up in Havana harbor (it caught fire all by itself). — The first time we were lied into a major war by a president was probably the Mexican-American war of 1846 when President James Polk lied that we’d been invaded by Mexico. Even Abraham Lincoln, then a congressman from Illinois, called him out on that lie . — You could also argue that when President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830 leading to the Trail of Tears slaughter and forced relocation of the Cherokee under President Buchanan (among other atrocities) it was all based on a series of lies. Bush’s lies that took us into Afghanistan and, a bit over a year later into Iraq, are particularly egregious, however, given his and Cheney’s reasons for those lies. In 1999, when George W. Bush decided he was going to run for president in the 2000 election, his family hired Mickey Herskowitz to write the first draft of Bush’s autobiography, A Charge To Keep . Although Bush had gone AWOL for about a year during the Vietnam war and was thus apparently no fan of combat, he’d concluded (from watching his father’s “little 3- day war” with Iraq) that being a “wartime president” was the most consistently surefire way to get reelected (if you did it right) and have a two-term presidency. “I’ll tell you, he was thinking about invading Iraq in 1999,” Herskowitz told reporter Russ Baker in 2004. “One of the things [Bush] said to me,” Herskowitz said, “is: ‘One of the keys to being seen as a great leader is to be seen as a commander-in-chief. My father had all this political capital built up when he drove the Iraqis out of (Kuwait) and he wasted it. “[Bush] said, ‘If I have a chance to invade Iraq, if I had that much capital, I’m not going to waste it. I’m going to get everything passed I want to get passed and I’m going to have a successful presidency.’” The attack on 9/11 gave Bush his first chance to “be seen as a commander-in-chief” when our guy Osama Bin Laden, who the Reagan/Bush administration had spent $3 billion building up in Afghanistan , engineered an attack on New York and DC. The crime was planned in Germany and Florida and on 9/11 Bin Laden was, according to CBS News, not even in Afghanistan : “CBS Evening News has been told that the night before the Sept. 11 terrorists attack, Osama bin Laden was in Pakistan. He was getting medical treatment with the support of the very military that days later pledged its backing for the U.S. war on terror in Afghanistan.” When the Obama administration finally caught and killed Bin Laden, he was back in Pakistan, the home base for the Taliban. But attacking our ally Pakistan in 2001 would have been impossible for Bush, and, besides, nearby Afghanistan was an easier target, being at that time the second-poorest country in the world with an average annual per-capita income of $700 a year. Bin Laden had run terrorist training camps there — unrelated to 9/11 — and they made a fine excuse for Bush’s first chance to “be seen as a commander-in-chief” and get some leadership cred. Cheney, meanwhile, was in a world of trouble because of a huge bet he’d made as CEO of Halliburton in 1998. Dresser Industries was big into asbestos and about to fall into bankruptcy because of asbestos lawsuits that the company was fighting through the court system. Cheney bet Dresser would ultimately win the suits and had Halliburton buy the company on the cheap, but a year later, in 1999, Dresser got turned down by the courts and Haliburton’s stock went into freefall, crashing 68 percent in a matter of months. Bush had asked Cheney — who’d worked in his father’s White House as Secretary of Defense — to help him find a suitable candidate for VP. Cheney, as his company was collapsing, recommended himself for the job. In July of 2000, Cheney walked away with $30 million from the troubled company and the year after that, as VP, Halliburton subsidiary KBR received one of the first no-bid no-ceiling (no accountability and no limit on how much they could receive) multi-billion-dollar military contracts. Bush and Cheney both had good reason to want to invade Afghanistan in October 2001. Bush was seen as an illegitimate president at the time because his father’s corrupt appointee on the Supreme Court, Clarence Thomas, had cast the deciding vote in the Bush v Gore lawsuit that made him president; a war that gave him legitimacy and the aura of leadership. Cheney’s company was in a crisis, and Afghanistan War no-bid contracts helped turn around Halliburton from the edge of bankruptcy into one of the world’s largest defense contractors today. Even Trump had to get into the “let’s lie about Afghanistan” game, in his case to have bragging rights that he’d “ended the war in Afghanistan.” In 2019, Trump went around the Afghan government (to their outrage: he even invited the Taliban to Camp David in a move that disgusted the world) to cut a so-called “peace deal” that sent thousands of newly-empowered Taliban fighters back into the field, and then drew down our troops to the point where today’s ongoing chaos in that country was absolutely predictable. Trump’s deal was the signal to the 300,000+ Afghan army recruits we’d put together and paid that America no longer had their back and if the Taliban showed up they should just run away. Which, of course, is what happened on Trump’s watch. As Susannah George of The Washington Post noted : “The Taliban capitalized on the uncertainty caused by the [Trump] February 2020 agreement reached in Doha, Qatar, between the militant group and the United States calling for a full American withdrawal from Afghanistan. Some Afghan forces realized they would soon no longer be able to count on American air power and other crucial battlefield support and grew receptive to the Taliban’s approaches.” Jon Perr’s article at Daily Kos did a great summary, with the title: “ Trump put 5,000 Taliban fighters back in battle and tied Biden’s hands in Afghanistan .” Trump schemed and lied to help his own 2020 reelection efforts, and the people who worked with our military and the US-backed Afghan government paid a terrible price for it. And now Trump’s using ICE to deport them from America, compounding that disgusting betrayal. As President Biden told America: “When I came to office, I inherited a deal cut by my predecessor—which he invited the Taliban to discuss at Camp David on the eve of 9/11 of 2019—that left the Taliban in the strongest position militarily since 2001 and imposed a May 1, 2021 deadline on U.S. Forces. Shortly before he left office, he also drew U.S. Forces down to a bare minimum of 2,500. “Therefore, when I became President, I faced a choice—follow through on the deal, with a brief extension to get our Forces and our allies’ Forces out safely, or ramp up our presence and send more American troops to fight once again in another country’s civil conflict. I was the fourth President to preside over an American troop presence in Afghanistan—two Republicans, two Democrats. I would not, and will not, pass this war onto a fifth.” America has been lied into too many wars. It’s cost us too much in money, credibility, and blood. We must remember the lies, and tell our children about them so that memory isn’t lost. When President Ford withdrew US forces from Vietnam (I remember it well), there was barely a mention of McNamara’s and LBJ’s lies that got us into that war. Similarly, today’s reporting on the chaos in Afghanistan and the ongoing conflict around the Iraqi oil fields almost never mention Bush’s and Cheney’s lies and ulterior motives in getting us into those wars in the first place. George Santayana famously noted, “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” We can’t afford to let these lies go down the memory hole, like we have the other wars we were lied into that I mentioned earlier. Sadly, it’s clear now that neither Bush nor Cheney will be held accountable for their lies or for the American, Afghan, and Iraqi blood and treasure they cost. But both should be subject to a clear and public airing of the crimes they committed in office and Bush should be required — at the very least — to apologize to the thousands of American families destroyed by the loss of their soldier children, parents, and spouses in those unnecessary wars, as well as to the people of both Afghanistan and Iraq. If the media refuses to mention the Bush/Cheney lies on this anniversary of 9/11, it’s all the more important that the rest of us use this opportunity to do so. Pass it on. https://www.edp24.co.uk/news/26617902.li.text: Court Norwich Lives "shattered" and "broken" by Norwich drink drive death Court Norwich By Peter Walsh Court and Crime Correspondent Share 8 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A police officer held a young Norwich man's hand as he "drew his last breath" after being run over by a drink-driver on Christmas Eve, a court heard. Thomas Plane, 28, died after Nicolae Brica's Renault Megane struck him and his twin brother James in Barrack Street in the early hours of December 24 last year. Norwich Crown Court heard Thomas became trapped beneath the vehicle and was dragged along the road before firefighters winched the car away so paramedics could reach him. Sentencing Brica on Thursday, Judge Andrew Shaw paid tribute to the officer who stayed with Thomas as he lay trapped under the car, holding his hand until he died. P:olice at scene of fatal crash (Image: Newsquest) Norwich Crown Court heard the 28-year-old twins had been riding a Beryl bike on their way back from a night out in the city with others - including older brother Ben - when they came off and "fell into the road". Thomas was injured and left "lying in the road" while his brother James had "gone to his aid". Another driver, who saw what had happened, stopped to try and warn other motorists of the brothers being in the road as James called 999. But Stephen Donnelly, prosecuting, said the call was "abruptly" cut short as James was "hit by the defendant's car mid-call". He said James was "thrown forward" after being struck by Brica while Thomas "became trapped underneath the vehicle and dragged along the road before the vehicle came to a stop". Emergency services arrived although paramedics were unable to reach Thomas until the car was winched out of the way by firefighters. The court heard one of the officers "stayed with him" as he was trapped under the car and "held his hand as he drew his last breath". P:olice at scene of fatal crash (Image: Newsquest) Mr Donnelly said Thomas was pronounced dead at the scene while James was taken to hospital with serious injuries, including fractures to his left leg, hip, base of spine and a dislocated left shoulder. Brica, formerly of Heathgate, Norwich, was arrested after he failed a breath test at the scene where he provided a reading of 72 microgames of alcohol in 100ml of breath. The legal limit is 35. He claims he had a glass of wine in the evening "after a few drinks" - believed to be beer - earlier in day. The evidential reading, taken later in custody was 68 micrograms of alcohol in 100ml of breath. Nicolae Brica (Image: Norfolk Constabulary) He made a number of significant remarks to officers, including "did he die", "I'm sorry" and "I don't know what happened, it was my fault". The 48-year-old went onto make further comments to officers, stating: "I killed one person. It's my fault". The Romanian national, who spoke through an interpreter, was in 2022 disqualified from driving for 17 months after being caught drink driving in the city in November 2021. He appeared for sentencing on Thursday (October 8) after he previously admitted causing death by careless driving while over the legal limit for alcohol. He also admitted causing serious injury by careless driving as well as driving while over the legal limit for alcohol. The court heard heart-breaking and deeply moving impact statements from six members of Thomas' devastated family before Brica was sentenced. Judge Andrew Shaw said the defendant was "obviously drunk" when he crashed into the brothers, killing one and seriously injuring the other. Judge Andrew Shaw (Image: Newsquest) He said the case was an "awful tragedy" in which Mr Plane's "vibrant young life" was brought to an end by Brica's "criminal careless driving while you were two times over the legal limit (for alcohol)." Imposing a seven-and-a-half-year prison sentence on Brica, he said the Romanian defendant, who also had a previous speeding offence from 2024, had "paid but scant regard to our driving laws and regulations". Norwich Crown Court (Image: Peter Walsh, Newsquest) Judge Shaw said Thomas's family had described with "remarkable courage" the "caring, talented, vibrant and funny young man" he was and how their lives would "never be the same again" now he was gone. He also paid tribute to the female police officer who attended the scene of the crash and remained close to Thomas under the car "holding his hand as he drew his last breath". Brica, who is likely to be deported once he has served his sentence, was also disqualified from driving for 10 years. LIVES FOREVER CHANGED Among those making moving statements about Thomas were his girlfriend Georgina, twin brother James, sister Molly, mother Catherine, father Stephen and older brother Ben. Each heart-wrenching statement read out in court movingly described their pain, suffering and loss. Roses left at the scene of fatal crash (Image: Peter Walsh, Newsquest) Georgina, who had wanted to marry Thomas and start a family with him, said: "I've had my heart broken and my entire world shattered." She touchingly described how Thomas "was my home" and how she "always felt safe with him" but how "I don't want to do anything now because Thomas is missing out". Thomas' twin said he had a "bond like no other" with his brother and "cannot put into words how much I loved Thomas - he meant everything to me". He said his life is now "forever changed" and "all I want to do is speak to Thomas". While his mother Catherine, who went out looking for her sons and came across the scene of the crash, said: "My heart is broken and my whole world has collapsed around me." Older brother Ben said the lives of his family have been "ripped apart" by Thomas' death and "shattered" by his loss and will "never be the same". Thomas's father Stephen said their son did not come home "because of what a drink driver did". He said Christmas had always been such an important family time but was now full of "grief" and "loss". Thomas' sister Molly said her "heart breaks" for the loss of the brother she "missed him so much". Rob Pollington, mitigating, said these sort of offences "ruin multiple lives". He said Brica, in getting behind the wheel after having a drink, "knows what he has done". "He understands what he has taken from others as a result of what he's done," he said. "He expects and understands that a custodial sentence has to be imposed in this case and that will be of some length". He said Brica had admitted the offences, sparing the family the ordeal of having to go through a trial, and was "extremely sorry". He added: "If he could swap places with Thomas Plane he would." ONE POOR CHOICE CAN CHANGE LIVES FOREVER Speaking after the sentencing hearing, DC Dylan Thomas, said: “This was a truly devastating incident which has had a lifelong impact on this family. "A young man lost his life and his twin brother suffered serious injuries, all as a result of a driver choosing to get behind the wheel after drinking alcohol. “Our thoughts remain with their family and loved ones, who have shown immense dignity throughout this investigation and court process. We hope today’s sentence provides them with some measure of closure. Nicolae Brica at an earlier court hearing (Image: Newsquest) “This tragedy was entirely preventable. Brica made the decision to drive after drinking alcohol, and that decision had catastrophic consequences. We would urge everyone to think carefully before getting behind the wheel after drinking. One poor choice can change lives forever.” Court Norwich Share Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading...
